extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, researchers and policymakers interested in Jamaican media law, censorship, and cultural policy
extracted.subtask_description: Summary of legal, regulatory, and social standards that have governed or justified censorship in Jamaica across broadcasting, music (dancehall), film, and street art. Includes specific regulatory provisions, examples of enforcement, and critiques about vagueness and freedom of expression tensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jamaica Broadcasting Commission (JBC) regulatory remit
rubrics_metrics.description: JBC aims to regulate and monitor the media industry and 'runs with full power of the regulation making and the control of the programming’s standard and technical quality.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implies the commission is responsible for setting programming standards, technical quality and exercising regulatory oversight over broadcasters; used as the basis for content bans and enforcement actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory framework implemented by the JBC
rubrics_metrics.description: The Jamaica Broadcasting Commission implements two broadcasting laws: the Broadcasting and Radio Re-diffusion Amendment Act and the Television and Sound Broadcasting Regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These laws and regulations constitute the legal basis for censorship/enforcement decisions and define what licensees may or may not broadcast.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulation 30(d) — prohibition on indecent or profane matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Quoted on the page: 'No licensee shall permit to be transmitted d) any indecent or profane matter, so, however, that any broadcast to which regulation 26 relates shall be deemed not to be indecent; Reg. 30(d)'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to justify bans on sexually explicit or vulgar material; however the page notes vagueness and enforcement difficulty. Example application: used in the ban on 'daggering' music.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulation 30(l) — prohibition on portrayals of violence offensive to good taste/public morality
rubrics_metrics.description: Quoted on the page: '(l) any portrayal of violence which offends against good taste, decency or public morality. Reg. 30(l)'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied to limit broadcasts that depict violence judged to offend public morality; enforcement depends on subjective standards of 'good taste' and 'public morality.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Ban on 'daggering' music as an application of the regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: JBC placed a ban on 'daggering' music (Feb 6, 2009); 'daggering' involves explicit lyrics discussing sex and homosexuality and was judged to violate Regulation 30(d) and Regulation 30(l).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an example of how the JBC applies the indecency and violent-portrayal provisions to dancehall content; the page frames it as content that combines explicit sexual content and portrayals that could offend public morality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural/historical sensitivity as a criterion for film censorship
rubrics_metrics.description: The Jamaican Cinematographic Authority censored a scene in Amistad (a slave ship revolt) as 'inappropriate for Jamaican audiences' given Jamaica's history of colonialism and slavery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorities may judge material inappropriate based on national historical sensitivity; the page records criticism (e.g., Rex Nettleford) that such censorship can 'control public and conceal historical truths' and be a 'conspiracy of silence.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Removal of street art justified by perceived public danger vs constitutional freedom
rubrics_metrics.description: Police have removed murals they perceive as 'dangerous to society' (carrying paintbrushes or spray paint to censor), while critics view removal as 'violent censorship' against freedom of expression under the Jamaican Constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enforcement actions against street art are often framed by authorities in terms of public order/safety, but critics treat removal as a suppression of political/community expression; the tension is a practical criterion in decisions about graffiti/murals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vagueness of broadcasting regulations and enforcement difficulty
rubrics_metrics.description: The article notes that 'broadcasting regulation contains some very vague clauses, like Regulation 30(d) and Regulation 30(l)... which causes more difficult for JBC of dealing with the related issues.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlights that ambiguous wording (e.g., 'indecent', 'good taste', 'public morality') complicates consistent application and legal analysis of censorship decisions; suggests a criterion of clarity/legal certainty for good regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference to freedom of the press principles as an informal check
rubrics_metrics.description: The commission has 'informally adopted the principles of the Freedom of the Press clause contained in the United States' first amendment.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicates an aspirational or informal standard influencing JBC practice — balancing regulatory restrictions against press freedom principles even if not codified in Jamaican law.
